title: How do people plan for the future?
essentialQuestion: How can saving, spending, budgeting and opportunity cost shape everyday decisions?
learningGoal: Make a simple, flexible plan for a small goal using saving, budgeting and trade-offs.

warmUp.question: What is one small thing you would like to be able to do one month from now?
options: Read a short book in English

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: What does each person give up now to reach their goal later?

cases.name: Mei's reading goal
cases.body: Goal: read a short English storybook by herself in four weeks. Plan A: read for 15 minutes every evening. Plan B: if the evening is busy, read at lunchtime instead.

cases.name: Sami's notebook goal
cases.body: Goal: buy a notebook and two pens for English class. Plan: when Sami gets a few coins, he puts half of them in a tin at home. He buys fewer sweets.

cases.name: The Friday savings group
cases.body: A group of 10 neighbours meets every Friday. Each person puts in the same small amount. Each week, one person takes all of it, until everyone has had a turn. Rosa used her turn to buy a water filter for her home.

cards.title: Mei's time budget for one evening

sections.heading: Spending now and saving for later
sections.text: Some choices affect only today, but others affect what we can do later. To spend means to use money or another resource to get something now, such as food or a bus ride. Spending is not bad, because everyone needs some things now. To save means to keep some money or resources for later. Saving is hard when there is not much, but small amounts can add up over time. Sami puts a few coins in a tin at home until he has enough for a notebook. In some communities, neighbours save together in a group. Each person puts a small amount into the group every week, and each week one person takes it all.
sections.simpler: Some choices are for today. Some are for later. To spend is to use money or things now. Everyone needs to spend on some things, like food. To save is to keep some money or things for later. Many small amounts make a bigger amount. Sami puts a few coins in a tin. Soon he can buy a notebook. Some neighbours save as a group. Each person puts in a little every week. Each week, one person takes it all.

sections.heading: A budget is a plan
sections.text: A budget is a plan for how to use money or time. It helps you compare what you have with what you need and want. Budgets are not only for money. Mei makes a time budget for her evenings. She plans time to help with dinner, to rest and to read English for 15 minutes. Budgeting is really about choices, and every choice has an opportunity cost. If Mei reads for 15 minutes, she has 15 fewer minutes for games on the shared phone. This is a trade-off: giving up one thing to get another. A careful budget helps you see your trade-offs before you choose.
sections.simpler: A budget is a plan for your money or time. It helps you see what you have and what you need. Mei makes a time budget for her evenings. She helps with dinner. She rests. She reads English for 15 minutes. So she has less time for games on the phone. That is a trade-off. You give up one thing to get another.

sections.heading: Small goals and flexible plans
sections.text: A goal is something you want to do or get, and you work towards it step by step. Nobody can control everything about the future, and plans can change when things around us change. That is why small, short goals are useful. They are goals you can work on now, such as learning 10 new English words a week, practising a skill or staying healthy. A strong plan is also flexible. Mei's Plan A is to read every evening. Her Plan B is to read at lunchtime if the evening gets busy. A flexible plan still works when life changes.
sections.simpler: A goal is something you want to do or get. You work towards it step by step. No one can control the future. Plans can change. So small goals help. You can work on them now. For example, you can learn 10 new words a week. A strong plan is flexible. Mei's Plan A is to read in the evening. If the evening is busy, she reads at lunch. That is her Plan B.

glossary.definition: To use money or other things to get something now.
glossary.example: Sami could spend his coins on sweets today.

glossary.definition: To keep money or other things so you can use them later.
glossary.example: Sami saves coins in a tin for a notebook.

glossary.definition: A plan for how to use your money or your time.
glossary.example: Mei's time budget shows 15 minutes for reading English.

glossary.definition: Giving up one thing so that you can have another.
glossary.example: Fewer phone games for more reading time is Mei's trade-off.

glossary.definition: Something you want to do or get, and work towards.
glossary.example: Mei's goal is to read a short storybook by herself.

glossary.definition: Able to change easily when things change.
glossary.example: Mei's plan is flexible because she has a Plan B.

options.text: Using all the phone data on the first day
options.feedback: Not quite. Using all the data at once is spending it now. Look for something kept for later.

options.text: Spending all the money on sweets at once
options.feedback: Not quite. That is spending everything now. Look for something kept for later, like Sami's coins.

options.text: Keeping a few coins in a tin for later
options.feedback: Yes. Keeping coins to use later is saving, just like Sami does for his notebook.

checks.question: Why does Mei have a Plan B?

options.text: So she can stop reading when it gets hard
options.feedback: Not quite. Plan B helps Mei keep reading. Read the part about flexible plans again.

options.text: So she can still read if her day changes
options.feedback: Yes. If the evening is busy, Mei reads at lunchtime. Her plan is flexible, so it still works.

options.text: So she can play more games on the shared phone
options.feedback: Not quite. Plan B is about reading at a different time. Read the part about flexible plans again.

write.prompt: Make a simple plan for Mei, Sami or another learner with one small goal. Include what they save or give up, the trade-off and a Plan B.
sentenceStarters: Each day or week, they will...
They will save or give up...
If things change, Plan B is...
selfCheck: I said what they save or give up.
write.example: The goal is for Sami to buy a notebook and two pens for English class. Each week, he will put half of any coins he gets into a tin at home. He will save these coins and give up some sweets. The trade-off is fewer sweets now, but a notebook later. If things change, Plan B is to ask the learning centre for a spare notebook he can use until he has saved enough.

speak.partnerTask: A youth group has a small amount of money for one activity: a sports day, a reading corner or a clean-up. Choose one together and name the opportunity cost.
speak.independentTask: Say: “A small goal I could work on is ___. My first step is ___.” You can choose a goal for Mei or Sami instead.

watch.title: Economics for Kids: Saving and Spending
watch.why: It explains saving and spending with simple examples and pictures.
watch.beforeQuestion: When is it better to spend now, and when is it better to save for later?
watch.afterQuestion: How can spending and saving both be useful?
watch.summary: This short video for younger learners explains spending and saving. People use money to get the things they need and want. But no one can have everything they want. This is called scarcity, so people must make choices. People usually get what they need before what they want. For example, the speaker needs a healthy lunch but wants a cupcake. So lunch comes first. Then the speaker checks if there is money left for the cupcake. When you spend, you get something now. But it may be small, and you may have little money left. When you save, you have to wait, and that can be hard. But later you can get something that costs more. There is no one right answer. Think about the good and bad sides of each choice.
keyPoints: Spending means using money to get something now.
Saving means waiting, so you can get something that costs more later.
There is no one right answer: think about the good and bad sides of each choice.

visual.description: A goal path drawn as stepping stones. On the left, Mei stands at the start. Four stones lead to a small flag on the right labelled 'Goal: read a storybook in four weeks'. Each stone is labelled 'Week 1' to 'Week 4' and shows a tiny book. Above the stones, the main path is labelled 'Plan A: read 15 minutes each evening'. A short side path branches off at Week 2 and joins the main path again, labelled 'Plan B: read at lunchtime if the evening is busy'. A small note beside the path shows a phone with a minus sign and the words 'Trade-off: fewer phone games'.
visual.alt: A path of stepping stones leads to Mei's reading goal. A side path shows her Plan B, which joins the main path again, and a note shows her trade-off of fewer phone games.

DCMP: Economics for Kids video series

sensitiveNotes: The lesson avoids pay, bank accounts, loans and long career plans on purpose. Keep discussion to small, short goals that learners can control. Do not ask learners where they will live in future or about their household's money. If a learner finds talk about the future upsetting, return to the small goals in the lesson and do not press.
The video opens by saying that many people earn money by working, and its examples are a cupcake, an ice cream and a toy. Preview it; the written summary leaves out the part about working.
educatorNotes: The Friday savings group is a rotating savings group. These are found in many parts of the world under local names; the FAO source lists, for example, susu (Ghana), arisan (Indonesia), ekub (Ethiopia) and tontines (West Africa). A partner can use a local name. Present it as something adults organise, based on trust, not as advice for learners to join one.
Sami's tin, Mei's time budget and Rosa's water filter can be swapped for local examples, such as saving phone credit or data, or planning study time around chores and classes.
changes: Added a fictional evidence set (three small plans and a time budget), a warm-up, an example answer, a self-check and a visual plan, which were missing.
Changed three multiple-choice checks to two choice questions and one open think question, with the correct answers in different positions.

Adapted for learners who may have no income, bank account or settled future: examples use coins in a tin, a neighbourhood savings group, a time budget and short goals. Removed rent, allowance and 'long-term' planning.
Added a new section on small goals and flexible plans (Plan A and Plan B), so the lesson does not assume a stable future.
Glossary now spend, save, budget, trade-off, goal and flexible, all used in both versions of the text. Dropped 'short-term choice' and 'long-term choice'.
Rewrote the simpler English so it is much simpler, and rewrote the video summary so it stands alone.
Lightly edited the essential question (removed a comma only) and removed the stale nextLesson field.
